identity.title: How much of my dataset did you use? Quantitative Data Usage Inference in Machine Learning

problem.claim: Determine what proportion of a dataset was used to train a machine-learning model.

gap.claim: Prior work framed usage inference as binary all-or-none or any-or-none decisions, which the authors describe as fragile for real, non-binary usage risks.

contributions.claim: Introduces Dataset Usage Cardinality Inference (DUCI), a fine-grained analysis for estimating the exact proportion of data used.
Presents an algorithm that leverages debiased membership guesses for dataset-usage estimation.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish DUCI from binary usage inference by targeting fine-grained, proportion-level estimation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their algorithm matches the performance of the optimal MLE approach, with maximum error below 0.1.
The authors report substantially lower computational cost than the optimal MLE approach, citing an example of 300× less computation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Asks how much of a dataset was used to train a machine-learning model.
Connects quantitative usage assessment to data owners' unauthorized-use risk and identifies the limitations of binary formulations.
Proposes DUCI to estimate the exact usage proportion.
Reports MLE-matched performance with maximum error below 0.1 at much lower computational cost, including a 300× example.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly contrasts binary usage inference with proportion-level estimation and pairs the proposed method with a reported maximum error and a computational-cost comparison.

lessons.interpretation: A strong abstract can make the task distinction concrete by aligning the representation of the problem with directly comparable evidence.
lessons.application: When replacing a coarse binary task, define the finer-grained target numerically and report matched quality and resource metrics against a relevant baseline.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the operational decision is genuinely binary or when the target proportion cannot be measured or interpreted reliably.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the evaluation setting, datasets, sample sizes, or conditions under which the maximum error and 300× cost reduction were obtained.
It does not define the exact error metric, the computational-cost measure, or how the optimal MLE baseline was configured.

editorial_revisions.before: The abstract explicitly contrasts binary usage inference with proportion-level estimation and pairs the proposed method with both an error bound and a computational-cost comparison.
editorial_revisions.after: The abstract explicitly contrasts binary usage inference with proportion-level estimation and pairs the proposed method with a reported maximum error and a computational-cost comparison.
